title: Project Management Fundamentals
summary: Plan and run projects: scope, work breakdown, scheduling and critical path, budgets and earned value, risk, communication and closing.
audience: Aspiring project managers, team leaders, students and small-business owners

lessons.title: What a project is and how it is managed

body.p: A project is a temporary effort to create a unique product, service or result. It has a start, an end and a goal. This sets it apart from routine operations, which repeat, such as running a shop each day. Building a clinic, launching a mobile app or organising a school conference are all projects.

Every project is limited by scope (what must be delivered), time (the deadline) and cost (the budget). Quality sits in the middle. A change in one affects the others. If a client adds features, the project will usually need more time or money, or something else must be cut.

list: Initiating: agree the purpose, sponsor and main goals.
Planning: define the work, schedule, budget, risks and team.
Executing: do the work and manage the team.
Monitoring and controlling: track progress and fix problems early. This runs alongside the other phases.
Closing: hand over, get acceptance, record lessons learned.

body.tip: A project manager is responsible for results but rarely does all the work. The job is to plan, coordinate, communicate and remove obstacles.

lessons.title: Defining scope and breaking down the work

body.p: Scope is the full list of work needed to deliver the project. A clear scope statement says what is included, what is excluded, and how success will be measured. Vague scope is the main cause of scope creep, where extra work is added without changing time or budget.

A work breakdown structure, or WBS, divides the project into smaller parts until each piece can be estimated, assigned and tracked. For a school website, the top level may be Design, Build, Content and Launch. Under Build you might list Home page, Contact page and Admin login. The smallest items are called work packages.

list: Each item should have one owner.
Deliverables are things, such as a design file or a trained team, not activities.
The total of the parts must equal the whole: nothing missing and nothing extra.

body.tip: Write down acceptance criteria for each deliverable, for example: the page loads in under 3 seconds on a mobile phone.

body.p: A schedule shows what happens when. First list activities, their durations and their dependencies. The most common dependency is finish-to-start: Task B cannot start until Task A finishes.

The critical path is the longest chain of dependent activities, and it sets the shortest possible project time. Any delay on the critical path delays the whole project. Other activities have float, also called slack, which is how long they can slip without delaying the end.

Example: Task A takes 3 days. After A, Task B takes 4 days and Task C takes 2 days. Task D takes 3 days and needs both B and C to finish. The path A-B-D takes 3 + 4 + 3 = 10 days. The path A-C-D takes 3 + 2 + 3 = 8 days. The critical path is A-B-D at 10 days, and Task C has 2 days of float.

list: Gantt chart: a bar chart showing tasks against time.
Milestone: a key point in the schedule with zero duration, such as 'Design approved'.
Add buffer where uncertainty is high, but state it openly.

body.p: A budget is built by estimating the cost of each work package: labour, materials, equipment, travel and a reserve for the unexpected. Estimates improve as the project becomes clearer. Ask people who have done similar work, and compare with past projects.
For uncertain tasks, give an optimistic, most likely and pessimistic value. A simple average of the three gives a quick estimate. It forces the team to think about what could go wrong.

Earned value management compares planned work, completed work and spending. Suppose the budget for the project is 100,000. By now the plan said 40% should be done, so planned value is 40,000. Only 30% is done, so earned value is 30,000. You have spent 35,000, so actual cost is 35,000.

list: Schedule performance index (SPI) = earned value ÷ planned value = 30,000 ÷ 40,000 = 0.75. Below 1 means behind schedule.
Cost performance index (CPI) = earned value ÷ actual cost = 30,000 ÷ 35,000 = about 0.86. Below 1 means over budget.

body.p: A risk is an uncertain event that could help or harm the project. Risk management means identifying risks early, judging how likely and how serious they are, and deciding what to do about them. Keep a risk register: a list of risks with an owner and a response for each.

A simple method scores probability from 1 to 5 and impact from 1 to 5, then multiplies them. A risk with probability 4 and impact 3 scores 12. A risk with probability 3 and impact 5 scores 15, so it needs attention first.

list: Avoid: change the plan so the risk cannot happen.
Mitigate: reduce the chance or the effect.
Transfer: share the risk, for example with insurance or a contract.
Accept: do nothing now, but set aside a reserve.

body.p: Quality means meeting the agreed requirements. Plan quality in from the start through reviews, testing and checklists, rather than trying to inspect problems out at the end.

lessons.title: People, communication and closing a project

body.p: Projects are done by people. A stakeholder is anyone affected by or able to influence the project: the sponsor, users, team members, regulators and the community. List your stakeholders and decide how much each needs to be informed or involved.

list: Agree who gets which report, how often and by what channel.
Hold short regular meetings with a clear agenda and written actions.
Report problems early. Surprises damage trust far more than bad news delivered promptly.
Number of communication channels in a team of n people is n(n-1)/2, so 6 people have 15 links. It grows quickly, which is why structure matters.

body.p: Closing a project means getting formal acceptance, releasing the team, finishing payments and contracts, and archiving documents. Hold a lessons-learned session. Record what went well, what did not, and what to do differently, so the next project begins with better knowledge.

body.tip: Praise team members for good work in public and give corrective feedback in private.
